name: Autologous conditioned serum

card.summary: An injectable serum made from a person's own blood, rich in interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, used for joint and tissue inflammation and explored for jaw-joint comfort and skin rejuvenation.
card.note: Clinic-based injection; not FDA approved in the US.

quick.overview:
Autologous conditioned serum (ACS), sold as Orthokine, is made by incubating a person's blood and separating the serum, which is then rich in anti-inflammatory proteins such as interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. It is injected into inflamed joints or tissues.

Its link to appearance runs through recovery and comfort: calmer joints and tendons can support continued training, and jaw-joint (TMJ) injections are studied by oral surgeons. A separate blood-derived product has also been studied for skin aging.
quick.how: In clinics, blood is drawn, incubated and centrifuged, and the resulting serum is injected over a series of sessions into the target joint or area. It is performed by physicians; it is not a home practice.
quick.risks: As an injection it carries the usual procedural risks. The US FDA has not approved it, and a Wikipedia summary reports tentative evidence overall. Trials in knee osteoarthritis and TMJ conditions are the main published human data.

lead: Autologous conditioned serum (ACS), also called Orthokine and, in some clinics, Regenokine, is a blood-derived injectable. Blood is incubated and centrifuged to yield serum enriched in interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), a natural inhibitor of an inflammatory cytokine. It was developed in the mid 1990s and has been used in osteoarthritis, radicular pain and some tendon and muscle injuries.[1]

Its connection to how people look runs through recovery and joint comfort. Lifters, athletes and people recovering from procedures discuss it as a way to settle inflamed joints and tendons so that training can continue, and training volume is what builds and maintains physique. It has also been studied in jaw-joint (temporomandibular) conditions, which matter to people working on the jaw and face, and a related blood-secretome product has been tested for skin aging.[2][3][5]

The method became widely known beyond orthopedics in 2011 and 2012, when American sports media reported that basketball player Kobe Bryant and other athletes had travelled to Germany for it.[8][9] The best-known trial randomized 376 people with knee osteoarthritis to ACS or a control injection and reported on pain and function outcomes.[4] Wikipedia describes the evidence overall as tentative, and the treatment has no US FDA approval.[6]

chain: Own blood incubated to enrich IL-1Ra
Serum injected at an inflamed joint or tendon
Less joint inflammation allows continued training and recovery
angle.text: ACS targets inflammation in joints and soft tissue, which people in strength and jaw-surgery circles connect to recovery and keeping up training. A blood-secretome product from the same family has been tested for skin aging.

paras: About 60 ml of blood is drawn from a vein, incubated at a slightly raised temperature and centrifuged; the serum layer is then injected into the affected area. The treatment is often given as a series of injections.[6] Journalists covering the method described the incubation step as a kind of artificial fever that prompts blood cells to release anti-inflammatory proteins, and the yellowish serum as the layer that carries them.[8][9]

The central component is IL-1Ra, which blocks interleukin-1, a cytokine regarded as an important mediator of inflammation, pain and tissue breakdown in musculoskeletal disease.[1] A laboratory study of the serum's cytokine profile also examined its effects on cartilage cells in vitro and the levels reached in the joint after injection.[7] Unlike platelet-rich plasma (PRP), which concentrates platelets, ACS relies on incubating whole blood to raise cytokine levels, which Wikipedia notes as the main difference between the two.[6]

ACS was developed in the mid 1990s as a practical and relatively inexpensive way to generate IL-1Ra.[1] Wikipedia credits molecular biologist Julio Reinecke and Düsseldorf spinal surgeon Peter Wehling with the patented method, reports first approval of Orthokine in Germany in 2003, and says about 60,000 patients worldwide had received it by August 2012.[6]

A 2004 pilot study in sportsmen with muscle strains and a companion animal study using a muscle contusion model extended interest from joints to muscle injury, and a 2007 review in BioDrugs summarized the use of Orthokine therapy across orthopedic conditions.[10][11][12] In veterinary medicine, a 2007 experiment in horses with surgically induced osteoarthritis examined clinical, biochemical and tissue effects of intra-articular ACS.[13]

Coverage in 2011 and 2012 brought the treatment to a general audience. Grantland and other outlets reported that Kobe Bryant travelled to Düsseldorf for a version of the treatment for his right knee and returned for a second round, and that he reportedly recommended it to baseball player Alex Rodriguez.[8] Singularity Hub added that golfer Fred Couples had received it for back pain and credited it after a 2011 senior tournament win.[9] Fans nicknamed it the Kobe Procedure.[6]

The coverage explained why athletes travelled abroad: in the United States, human tissue products fall under drug rules unless minimally manipulated, and few American doctors offered it, though physician Chris Renna was reported to administer Regenokine at clinics in Dallas and Santa Monica.[8] Proponents quoted in the reports said such biologic therapies might help avoid surgery and shorten recovery. Renna was quoted as saying success rates near 90 percent were possible when it was combined with lifestyle changes.[8] The authors of both articles stressed that independent evidence was limited and that part of any benefit could be placebo, citing then-recent PRP trials as the nearest comparison.[8][9]

A review describes use for human and equine osteoarthritis and radicular compression, with interest in tendinopathy, muscle injury and tunnel widening after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction.[1] A registered phase 1 study enrolled 62 people to examine ACS after ACL reconstruction.[14] A 2023 protocol describes a randomized placebo-controlled trial (RADISAC) of ACS around the dorsal root ganglion in chronic radicular pain.[15]

A 2024 pilot randomized study compared ACS with dextrose prolotherapy in internal derangement of the temporomandibular joint,[2] and a 2026 randomized trial compared ACS with platelet-rich plasma after arthrocentesis in TMJ osteoarthritis.[3] A further registered trial enrolled 75 people with TMJ osteoarthritis.[16] For people concerned with jaw function after jaw procedures or heavy chewing-based routines, these studies are the closest research to the facial region.

A multi-center prospective study of Exokine, a cell-free blood cell secretome, reported on skin aging parameters.[5] A separate single-blinded randomized trial tested ACS as a dressing in hard-to-heal wounds against saline dressings.[17] Neither is a standard cosmetic use, and both concern related blood-derived preparations.
A single-center case series reported on Orthokine injection in classical trigeminal neuralgia, a facial pain condition.[18]

Wikipedia states that evidence is tentative, that ACS is not included in medical guidelines, and that the Osteoarthritis Research Society International has not recommended it.[6] Orthopedic professor Freddie Fu was quoted there as saying more high-quality independent trials were needed.[6] A 2019 review of orthobiologics for osteoarthritis places ACS alongside PRP and other products,[19] and a 2024 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons overview addresses PRP, the closest and better-studied comparator.[20] A 2016 review by authors involved in the method's development concluded that experience suggests ACS is safe and effective.[1]

Broader reviews of intra-articular therapies for knee osteoarthritis compare ACS with hyaluronic acid, corticosteroids and PRP,[21][22] and a 2023 randomized double-blind study compared ACS with triamcinolone in knee osteoarthritis.[23]

Because it is an injection into a joint or tissue, ACS carries the general procedural risks of such injections, and the product is produced from the patient's own blood to reduce immune reactions. It is approved in Germany but not by the US FDA, and the cost in 2012 was about 6,000 euros without health insurance coverage.[6] Wikipedia notes that clinics in the US have offered it despite the absence of approval, and that sports leagues have not banned it.[6][8]

The randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled knee osteoarthritis trial enrolled 376 patients and used intention-to-treat analysis.[4] Grantland reported that about two thirds of ACS patients in it described much greater relief against about a third in the control groups.[8] Other randomized work compares ACS with triamcinolone in knee osteoarthritis and with other injections in TMJ disorders.[2][3][23] A registered phase 2/3 study (15 participants) and a 2026 study comparing PRP with activated cytokine-rich serum are listed for knee osteoarthritis.[24][25] Case series have examined trigeminal neuralgia.[18]

lore.intro: ACS is mentioned in strength-training and injury forums as one of the biologic options alongside prolotherapy and PRP, usually as a pain and joint-recovery treatment rather than as a cosmetic one.[26]

claims.claim: ACS can calm arthritic joints enough to extend an athletic career
claims.believers: Athlete use by Bryant, Rodriguez and Couples is cited by supporters, and clinicians quoted in the press describe success rates of 75 to 90 percent.[8][9]
claims.experts: The 2009 randomized trial reported benefit in knee osteoarthritis,[4] while Wikipedia describes the broader evidence as tentative.[6]

claims.claim: Heating blood creates a healing fever that makes the serum regenerative
claims.believers: Proponents describe incubation as triggering a natural inflammatory healing response that concentrates anti-inflammatory proteins.[9]
claims.experts: Laboratory work has characterized the cytokine content of the serum and its effects on cartilage cells in vitro.[7]

claims.claim: It can substitute for surgery or steroid injections
claims.believers: Supporters argue biologic injections could avoid surgery and shorten recovery.[8]
claims.experts: A randomized double-blind study compared ACS with triamcinolone in knee osteoarthritis,[23] and reviews place it among several intra-articular options.[19][21]

claims.believers: Oral and maxillofacial researchers have treated TMJ problems with ACS as a more biologic alternative to other injections.[2]
claims.experts: Randomized trials compare ACS with prolotherapy and PRP; they are small and recent.[2][3]

claims.believers: Manufacturers and investigators of a related cell-free secretome describe improvements in skin aging parameters.[5]
claims.experts: The Exokine study is a single prospective multi-center study of a related product, not ACS itself.[5]

claims.believers: Some commentators on athlete use raise this possibility themselves.[8][9]
claims.experts: The 2009 trial used a blinded control group, which addresses placebo response in knee osteoarthritis.[4]
